title: Gold Mine Collapse in Sudan's West Kordofan Kills at Least 60
excerpt: The al-Zara artisanal mine disaster — with up to 82 dead reported and dozens missing — is the latest deadly collapse in a gold sector that funds Sudan's civil war.
body:
• A collapse at the al-Zara artisanal gold mine in West Kordofan, Sudan, has killed at least 60–70 miners, with some sources reporting up to 82 dead and dozens more missing.
  • The collapse began September 13 in one shaft and spread through interconnected shafts in fragile sandy soil; the site lacked basic safety measures and rescue equipment.
  • Only local residents are conducting rescue work — with hand tools and a single privately owned forklift — while authorities say miners may still be alive at depths beyond 30 meters.
  • Sudan is one of Africa's largest gold producers, and unregulated artisanal mining — a key revenue stream in the country's civil war — has a long record of deadly collapses.

A gold mine collapse in Sudan's West Kordofan state has killed at least 60 people, with some sources putting the toll as high as 82 and dozens more still missing, making it one of the deadliest mining disasters in the country's recent history. The collapse began Sunday, September 13, at the al-Zara mine — an informal artisanal site in the Fouja area northwest of al-Nuhud town — and spread through a series of interconnected shafts in fragile, sandy soil.

Accounts of the death toll vary by source: Reuters cited three local sources reporting at least 60 dead, Xinhua reported at least 63, the Associated Press cited the Sudan Doctors Network and survivors reporting at least 67, and an anonymous local administration official told AP that 82 bodies had been recovered. The Kordofan Observatory monitoring group said more than 70 were dead or missing. All sources agree the toll is expected to rise.

No rescue machinery, only hand tools

The rescue effort is being carried out almost entirely by local residents, digging with rudimentary tools through loose soil, with no specialized rescue teams on site. The Kordofan Observatory said only a single privately owned forklift was available, and rescuers have been unable to reach depths beyond 30 meters, where survivors may still be trapped underground.

"We do not have the machinery to lift dirt and stones and search for survivors at depths of more than 30 meters. There were dozens of people working in the mine."

— Khair al-Sayyed Gabara, survivor, to the Associated Press

The Sudan Doctors Network said the mine "lacked basic safety and protective measures." Survivor Al-Amin Suliman told AP that 60 bodies had been recovered as of Wednesday morning — "There are still people stuck inside."

A war economy built on gold

Sudan is one of Africa's largest gold producers — official figures put 2025 output at 70 tons, up from 64 tons in 2024, generating roughly $1.8 billion in revenue. Artisanal and small-scale mining produces the vast majority of that gold, around 80%, and more than half of output is smuggled out of the country, according to a 2024 UN panel of experts, with the UAE and Dubai the main destination.

Gold has become a key revenue source in Sudan's civil war. West Kordofan is under the control of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which Reuters, UN experts, and The Sentry report is deeply entrenched in artisanal mining in Darfur and Kordofan through the Al-Junaid company and protection rackets. A UN panel reported roughly $860 million in gold extracted from RSF-controlled areas in 2024, a figure that has been heavily disputed. Over 800 artisanal mining sites employ an estimated 1.5 to 2 million miners, with little regulation since the 2021 coup ended reform efforts.

A long record of deadly collapses

Deadly collapses at unregulated sites are frequent. A 2023 collapse killed 14 miners, a 2021 collapse at the Darsaya mine in West Kordofan killed 38, at least seven miners were killed in a Red Sea province collapse in August 2026, and 13 died in South Kordofan in January 2026. In a war-shattered country where formal oversight has collapsed, miners keep returning to the shafts because gold is one of the few reliable sources of income — and one of the war's most contested resources.

What comes next

The Kordofan Observatory has appealed for urgent rescue efforts, noting that at least one survivor reported others still alive underground. No statement has emerged from Sudan's central government or the state-run mining company. As recovery work continues with hand tools in unstable soil, the disaster adds to the toll of a conflict economy in which gold funds the fighting — and the miners pay for it with their lives.
